title: B2B cross-border — GBP → EUR via Wise Business
scenario: A UK SME pays a German supplier €950. Wise receives GBP via Faster Payments, converts at mid-market, pays out via SEPA Instant.

steps.narration: The SME initiates a £820 top-up from its Barclays account, destined for Wise.
Faster Payments moves the £820 from Barclays to Wise's GBP safeguarded account in ~15 seconds.
Wise Business receives the GBP, verifies the SME's KYB status, and routes to the FX engine.
Wise applies the 10:00 GMT mid-market rate (GBP/EUR = 1.1732) and charges a transparent 0.43% fee.
Wise releases €950 via SEPA Instant to the supplier's Deutsche Bank account.
The supplier sees €950 credited in under 10 seconds. Meanwhile Wise posts the movement to its GL.
GL entries: DR Client Funds GBP £820, CR FX Position GBP £820; DR FX Position EUR €950, CR Client Funds EUR €950. Books balance.

title: Card payment — contactless tap at a UK café
scenario: A customer taps a Visa debit card for £6.50. Gateway, processor, acquirer, network, issuer — all touched in seconds.

steps.narration: Customer taps a Visa debit card on the contactless terminal.
The terminal + gateway encrypt the card data and tokenise the PAN so the merchant never sees the 16 digits.
The processor packages the £6.50 auth request and sends it to Visa.
Visa routes the auth to the cardholder's issuer based on the BIN.
The issuing bank checks balance, fraud, and 3DS/SCA exemptions, then replies APPROVED.
The approval flows back through the network to the processor and acquirer. The café's receipt prints APPROVED.
At end of day the acquirer batches all auths and submits for settlement. Two days later £6.43 (net of interchange + acquirer fee) lands in the café's bank.
In the café's books: DR Stripe Clearing £6.50 on sale day; DR Cash £6.43, DR Fees £0.07, CR Stripe Clearing £6.50 on settlement day.

title: ACH / domestic — UK salary via Faster Payments
scenario: A UK employer pays £3,200 net salary to an employee. Same logical flow as ACH but over Faster Payments.

steps.narration: The employer submits a payroll batch at 5pm Thursday.
Each payment is pushed as a separate Faster Payment — real-time, 24/7, unlike US ACH batching.
The employer bank authenticates the batch under PSD2 SCA (a corporate token).
Funds settle between the two banks via the Bank of England RTGS rails behind Faster Payments.
The employee sees £3,200 credited within 30 seconds, even though it's past banking hours.

title: SWIFT wire — $50k USA → India, 2 correspondent hops
scenario: A Miami firm wires $50,000 to an Indonesian supplier. Two correspondent banks in between, sanctions screening at every hop.

steps.narration: The Miami bank debits the sender and prepares an ISO 20022 payment message.
Rich structured data travels with the payment — invoice reference, purpose code, full supplier address.
SWIFT carries the message to JPMorgan (the sender's USD correspondent).
JPMorgan receives the message and posts to its nostro/vostro accounts.
The Miami bank's nostro USD account at JPMorgan is debited $50k; Standard Chartered Singapore's vostro at JPMorgan is credited.
Each correspondent screens names against OFAC and UN lists; a false positive here can cost 48 hours.
Standard Chartered converts USD → IDR, pocketing a ~2% spread on top of mid-market.
The Indonesian bank credits the supplier. Total elapsed: 2 business days. Total fees: ~$75 visible + ~$1,000 invisible (spread).

title: PayFac — Shopify onboards a new sub-merchant
scenario: A boutique signs up for Shopify, accepts its first card within 5 minutes. Shopify Payments is the PayFac.

steps.narration: The boutique owner signs up and enters a business name, EIN, and bank account.
Shopify runs KYB checks automatically — Companies House lookup, UBO verification, director ID.
Shopify Payments enrols the boutique under its own master merchant agreement with the acquirer — no separate contract needed.
The boutique never touches card data — Shopify's gateway handles it, so the boutique qualifies for the simplest PCI scope (SAQ A).
First card sale: £40 processed by Stripe (Shopify's underlying processor).
Interchange of ~£0.20 flows to the issuer; scheme fee, processor fee, and Shopify's margin come off the top.
Two days later the net ~£39.00 lands in the boutique's bank via a daily Shopify Payments pay-out.

title: AR / AP cycle — invoice raised, paid, booked
scenario: A SaaS vendor invoices a UK customer £1,200. The customer pays 14 days later. Both sides' books move.

steps.narration: Vendor issues invoice on 1 March. Vendor books: DR AR £1,200, CR Revenue £1,200 (accrual).
Customer receives invoice. Customer books: DR Software Expense £1,200, CR AP £1,200.
Customer's AP clerk codes the invoice to GL 6200 (Software) — controls how it appears in the P&L.
On 15 March the customer's finance team releases the payment via Faster Payments.
Both sides' bank statements show the £1,200 move. The AP clerk does a three-way match: invoice ↔ GL ↔ bank.
Customer books: DR AP £1,200, CR Cash £1,200. Vendor books: DR Cash £1,200, CR AR £1,200. Both sets of books balance again.
